Sqlite.Auth.Password.name: Sqlite.Auth.Password

unions.name: HashError
unions.comment:
Errors that can happen while deriving a password hash.

- `ImportPbkdf2KeyError` happens when the plain-text password cannot be
imported as PBKDF2 key material.
- `Pbkdf2DeriveBitsError` happens when the PBKDF2 derivation itself fails.
- `TooManyIterations` happens raised when [`hash`](#hash) is asked for more rounds
than ten times the default. It carries the rejected count.

unions.name: Hashed
unions.comment: A password that has been hashed and is safe to persist.

unions.name: Outcome
unions.comment:
The outcome of validating a candidate password.

- [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) contains the verified user
[`Sqlite.Auth.Session.issue`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#issue) requires to issue a
session. 
- `Rejected` means the candidate did not match or the user has no password. 
- `Locked` means the password is temporarily locked after repeated failures.

unions.name: Password
unions.comment:
A password, with a phantom type state of either [`PlainText`](#PlainText) or
[`Hashed`](#Hashed). Only the hashed form can be saved to the database.

unions.name: PlainText
unions.comment: A password in plain text, as received from the user.

unions.name: ResetError
unions.comment:
The ways redeeming a reset token can go wrong. 

- `InvalidResetToken` is a token that matches no live row, whether it is unknown, 
already used, replaced, or expired. The caller cannot tell which, deliberately.
- `ResetStorageError` is a database fault.

unions.name: ValidateError
unions.comment:
An error when validating a password.

- `StorageError` is an underlying error in the Sqlite database.
- `VerificationError` is a fault in the stored hash itself; see
[`VerifyError`](#VerifyError) for the ways it can happen.

unions.name: VerifyError
unions.comment:
The ways a stored PHC string can fail to verify against other than a plain
mismatch.

- `ParsePhcStringError` is when the stored hash is not a valid PHC string.
- `UnknownDigestAlgorithm` is when the PHC string names a digest algorithm this
module does not support.
- `MissingSalt` is when the PHC string has no salt segment.
- `InvalidSalt` is when the salt segment is not valid base64.
- `SaltTooLong` is when the salt exceeds the accepted maximum length.
- `MissingHash` is when the PHC string has no hash segment.
- `InvalidHash` is when the hash segment is not valid base64.
- `HashLengthMismatch` is when the hash length does not match the digest
algorithm's native output size.
- `MissingIterations` is when the PHC string has no `i` (iterations) parameter.
- `InvalidIterations` is when the `i` parameter is not a valid integer.
- `IterationsTooLarge` is when the iteration count exceeds the accepted maximum.
- `RederiveError` is when re-deriving the candidate's hash fails; it wraps a
[`HashError`](#HashError).

aliases.name: Options
aliases.comment:
The options the password functions take.

- `iterations` is the PBKDF2 round count for new hashes. The `Crypto` library
enforces a minimum of `600000` for SHA-256. Lower values make [`hash`](#hash)
fail with a [`HashError`](#HashError). Values ten times the default (6000000 
or above) are also denied as `error`
- `maxFailedAttempts` and `lockoutDurationMillis` control the lockout.
- `resetTokenLifetimeMillis` is how long a reset token stays redeemable.
  Longer lifetimes forgive users who click late; shorter ones shrink the
  window a leaked link stays live. See [`requestReset`](#requestReset).
aliases.type: { iterations : Basics.Int, maxFailedAttempts : Basics.Int, lockoutDurationMillis : Basics.Int, resetTokenLifetimeMillis : Basics.Int }

values.name: add
values.comment:
Store a hashed password for the given user to the database, returning the 
user on success for further pipeline steps.

    User.new database secureContext
        |> Task.andThen (Username.new database alice)
        |> Task.andThen (Password.add database hashedPassword)
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Password Sqlite.Auth.Password.Hashed -> Sqlite.Auth.User.User -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.Auth.User.User

values.name: change
values.comment:
Replace a user's password. This requires the [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) type. A password
check with [`validate`](#validate) creates it, and so does verifying a live session
through [`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify). To
require the current password, check it with [`validate`](#validate) and pass along
the [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) that check returns.

Changing the password revokes the user's sessions and deletes any outstanding reset token.

All operations are completed in a SQLite transaction, preventing data corruption.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Password Sqlite.Auth.Password.Hashed -> Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified

values.name: defaultOptions
values.comment:
The default, recommended, options for password hashing.

    { iterations = 600000
    , maxFailedAttempts = 5
    , lockoutDurationMillis = 900000 -- 15 minutes
    , resetTokenLifetimeMillis = 1800000 -- 30 minutes
    }

values.name: delete
values.comment:
Remove a user's password and any outstanding reset token, leaving the
account without a password. Requires the [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) type,
which a password check with [`validate`](#validate) or a live session through
[`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify) creates.

Existing sessions are not revoked. They are a separate credential and keep
working until they expire. Deleting a password when there is none succeeds and
changes nothing. Both writes happen in one transaction.

values.name: fromString
values.comment:
Turn a `String` into a plain-text [`Password`](#Password), ready to
[`hash`](#hash), or to pass to [`validate`](#validate).

values.name: hash
values.comment:
Hash a plain-text password into a [`Password Hashed`](#Password) ready for
[`add`](#add). Uses PBKDF2-SHA256 with `options.iterations` rounds and a random
16-byte salt. Returns a `Password Hashed` that can then be saved to the database.

Iterations above ten times the default are rejected with
[`TooManyIterations`](#TooManyIterations), so the cost of every stored hash
stays bounded.

Note that the algorithm used to produce the password hash is SHA-256. This cannot
currently be changed.
values.type: Crypto.SecureContext -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Options -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Password Sqlite.Auth.Password.PlainText -> Task.Task Sqlite.Auth.Password.HashError (Sqlite.Auth.Password.Password Sqlite.Auth.Password.Hashed)

values.name: migrationV1
values.comment:
Initial migration required for functions in this module to operate. Adds
the `passwords` and `password_reset_tokens` tables. Both reference users, so
run this after [`Sqlite.Auth.User.migrationV1`](Sqlite.Auth.User#migrationV1).

The first statement creates the `passwords` table:

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS passwords (
        user_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
        password TEXT NOT NULL,
        created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        last_used INTEGER,
        failed_login_attempts_count INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (failed_login_attempts_count >= 0),
        locked_until INTEGER,
        FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
    );

- `user_id` is the primary key and references the users (in the
[`Sqlite.Auth.User`](Sqlite.Auth.User) module), so there is one password per user.
- `password` is the user's hashed password, stored in PHC string format.
- Both `created_at` and `updated_at` are posix timestamp values.
- `last_used` is a posix timestamp of the last successful check, or null if never.
- `failed_login_attempts_count` counts consecutive failed checks.
- `locked_until` is the posix timestamp the password stays locked until after
too many failures, or null when unlocked.

The second statement creates the `password_reset_tokens` table:

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS password_reset_tokens (
        reset_token TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
        user_id TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
        created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        expires_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
    );

- `reset_token` is the primary key and stores the SHA-256 hash of the token.
- `user_id` references the users and is `UNIQUE`, so there is at most one live
reset token per user.
- `created_at` is a posix timestamp, and `expires_at` is the posix timestamp the
token stops being redeemable.

values.name: requestReset
values.comment:
Creates a reset token for the given user and returns `{ token }` exactly once. 
It's intended for this token to be transmitted safely, such as being emailed to the 
user.

The token is a standard base64 string, so it can contain `+`, `/`, and `=`. This
library does not make the token safe for any particular transport: if it travels
in a URL or form field, encode it for that context and hand [`reset`](#reset)
back the exact original string.

A new request replaces any existing token for the same user, so the previous
link stops working immediately.

To reset the password using the generated token, use the [`reset`](#reset) function.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Options -> Sqlite.Auth.User.User -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error { token : String.String }

values.name: reset
values.comment:
Use a generated reset token to set a new password. No user is needed, because the
 token resolves the user itself.

If successful, this function deletes the token, replaces the password, and revokes
all sessions the user may have. This function returns [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified),
allowing you to issue a new session if you choose after a successful reset.

Note: A token can be redeemed only once and is invalid after redemption.

    Password.reset database secureContext
        { token = generatedToken
        , new = hashedNew -- `Password Hashed`
        }
        |> Task.andThen (Session.issue database secureContext sessionOptions)
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> { token : String.String, new : Sqlite.Auth.Password.Password Sqlite.Auth.Password.Hashed } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Auth.Password.ResetError Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified

values.name: validate
values.comment:
Check a plain-text password against a user's stored password. The user argument 
is the `Maybe` that [`Sqlite.Auth.Username.user`](Sqlite.Auth.Username#user) returns 
to make chaining easier. For example, you might handle user login like this:

    Username.user database givenUserName
        |> Task.andThen (Password.validate database secureContext options candidate)
        |> Task.andThen
            (\outcome ->
                when outcome is
                    Password.Verified proof ->
                        Session.issue database secureContext sessionOptions proof
                    ...
            )
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Options -> Sqlite.Auth.Password.Password Sqlite.Auth.Password.PlainText -> Maybe.Maybe Sqlite.Auth.User.User -> Task.Task Sqlite.Auth.Password.ValidateError Sqlite.Auth.Password.Outcome

Sqlite.Auth.Session.name: Sqlite.Auth.Session

unions.name: VerifyError
unions.comment:
Why a presented token failed to verify.

- `StorageError` is an underlying error in the Sqlite database.
- `TokenNotFound` is when the token matches no session row at all.
- `Revoked` is when the session has been revoked.
- `Expired` is when the session is past its absolute lifetime.
- `IdleTimeout` is when the session went unused for longer than `idleTimeoutMillis`.

aliases.name: Options
aliases.comment:
Options for sessions. `lifetimeMillis` is the maximum length the token is
valid for before expiring. `idleTimeoutMillis` is the maximum length the token
can exist without being used before expiring.

aliases.name: Session
aliases.type: { sessionToken : String.String, userId : String.String, createdAt : Basics.Int, expiresAt : Basics.Int, lastUsedAt : Basics.Int, revokedAt : Maybe.Maybe Basics.Int }

values.name: defaultOptions
values.comment:
The default, recommended, options for sessions.

    { lifetimeMillis = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 -- 30 days
    , idleTimeoutMillis = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 -- 7 days
    }

values.name: issue
values.comment:
Issue a session for a [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) user. You can 
obtain a `Verified` with a credential check such as what
[`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate) produces.

This function returns two things: the session and the token.

The session is the row saved to the database representing the session. This 
includes the hashed session token. This value is returned to be inspected, never 
to be sent to the client.

The token value is the raw token (not hashed). This value should be sent safely
to the user's browser. It's _highly_ recommended you send the token to the client 
as a cookie that is HttpOnly, Secure, and has SameSite=Lax rules. Without these 
rules, or if the raw token is saved via IndexedDB, localStorage, or other methods, 
it's vulnerable to being stolen by attacks.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Sqlite.Auth.Session.Options -> Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error { session : Sqlite.Auth.Session.Session, token : String.String }

values.name: list
values.comment:
List all of a given user's live sessions. Live is defined as sessions that
have not yet been revoked or are beyond their lifetimes.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> { userId : String.String } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error (Array.Array Sqlite.Auth.Session.Session)

values.name: migrationV1
values.comment:
Initial migration required for functions in this module to operate.

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (
        session_token TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
        created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        expires_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        last_used_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        revoked_at INTEGER,
        FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
    );

- `session_token` is the primary key and stores the SHA-256 hash of the token.
- `user_id` references the user's id.
- `created_at` is a posix timestamp, and `expires_at` is the posix timestamp the
session stops being valid.
- `last_used_at` is a posix timestamp of the last successful verification, used
to enforce the idle timeout.
- `revoked_at` is the posix timestamp the session was revoked, or null while live.

values.name: revoke
values.comment:
Revoke a session by its raw token. If the given token does not exist, the 
`Task` will succeed, but no changes will be made to the database.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Sqlite.Auth.Session.Options -> { token : String.String } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error {}

values.name: revokeAll
values.comment: Revoke every live session a user holds.

values.name: verify
values.comment:
Verify a presented token, succeeding with the [`Session`](#Session) and
the user whose session has been verified. A revoked, expired, or idle session, 
or a token matching no session at all — fails the task with the matching 
[`VerifyError`](#VerifyError).

The returned, `Verified`, user lets a live session authorize actions without 
re-checking a credential:

    Session.verify database secureContext options { token = token }
        |> Task.andThen .verified
        |> Task.andThen (Username.change database { from = old, to = new })

It's recommended session tokens are verified for each authenticated request, ensuring 
the user performing a specific action is able and allowed to do so.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Crypto.SecureContext -> Sqlite.Auth.Session.Options -> { token : String.String } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Auth.Session.VerifyError { session : Sqlite.Auth.Session.Session, verified : Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified }

Sqlite.Auth.User.name: Sqlite.Auth.User

aliases.name: User
aliases.comment:
A user that exists in the database. This does not mean the user has been
verified via credentials. It is simply a user that exists.

This value is produced by functions that create or look up a user, such as 
[`new`](#new), [`get`](#get), or 
[`Sqlite.Auth.Username.user`](Sqlite.Auth.Username#user).

This value is consumed by functions that read a user's id, attach a username
to a user, or check a password for a given user, such as [`id`](#id), 
[`Sqlite.Auth.Username.list`](Sqlite.Auth.Username#list), or
[`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate).

This value wraps an internal type that cannot be constructed by functions
outside of this package. If you want to get access to the underlying user
id this type holds, use the [`id`](#id) function.

aliases.name: Verified
aliases.comment:
A user that exists in the database and has been proven, via a credential
check or a live session, that they are the user they say they are. Unlike the
`User` type, which only proves a user exists, this proves the user has been
authenticated.

This value is produced by a credential check or a live-session verification, such 
as [`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate), 
[`Sqlite.Auth.Password.reset`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#reset), or
[`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify).

This value is consumed by privileged account operations, such as [`delete`](#delete),
[`Sqlite.Auth.Password.change`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#change), 
or [`Sqlite.Auth.Session.issue`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#issue).

This value wraps an internal type that cannot be constructed by functions
outside of this package. If you want to get access to the underlying user
id this type holds, use the [`verifiedId`](#verifiedId) function.

values.name: delete
values.comment:
Delete a user. This also deletes everything that references them including 
usernames, passwords, password reset tokens, and sessions, assuming the given
database has foreign keys enabled and you've used the migrations in this package
which contain `ON DELETE CASCADE` statements.

This operation requires a [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) user. A user
can be verified by validating their password 
([`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate)) or their 
current session ([`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify)).

Deleting a user who does not exist succeeds with no changes to the underlying
database.

values.name: get
values.comment:
Look up a user by id, returning the `User` for the row. The task
fails when there's no user with the given id.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> { id : String.String } -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.Auth.User.User

values.name: id
values.comment: Get the id of the given `User`.

values.name: migrationV1
values.comment:
Initial migration required for functions in this module to operate.

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (
        id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
        created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL
    );

The `users` table is used as a foreign key reference for _all_ other modules in this 
package. As such, it is required for most, if not all, of the functions in this package
to operate successfully.

values.name: new
values.comment:
Create a new user with a randomly generated UUID v4 identifier.

It's _highly_ recommended that you immediately create a 
[username](Sqlite.Auth.Username) for the new user in the same SQLite
transaction. After a user is created, the only method of retrieving
it from the database is by its id (via the [get](#get) function) or by
the user's created username. If you plan on using this package for user-facing
authentication, user ids are not the most friendly way to remember how
to log into an account!

values.name: verifiedId
values.comment: Get the id of a given `Verified` user.

Sqlite.Auth.Username.name: Sqlite.Auth.Username

unions.name: Normalized
unions.comment: A normalized username that is ready to be saved to the database.

unions.name: Username
unions.comment: A username, with a phantom type state of either `Raw` or `Normalized`.

values.name: change
values.comment:
Change one of a user's usernames to a new one. `from` names the username
being replaced and `to` the replacement. With the default schema, a user 
may hold several usernames, so only the row matching both the user and `from`
changes.

This operation requires a [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) user. A user
can be verified by validating their password 
([`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate)) or their 
current session ([`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify)).
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> { from : Sqlite.Auth.Username.Username Sqlite.Auth.Username.Normalized, to : Sqlite.Auth.Username.Username Sqlite.Auth.Username.Normalized } -> Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified

values.name: delete
values.comment:
Remove one username of a user.

This operation requires a [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) user. A user
can be verified by validating their password 
([`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate)) or their 
current session ([`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify)).
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Sqlite.Auth.Username.Username Sqlite.Auth.Username.Normalized -> Sqlite.Auth.User.Verified -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error {}

values.name: deleteAll
values.comment:
Remove all of a user's usernames. This may leave the user in a less-than-ideal
scenario if usernames are the only method of identifying themselves when logging
in. Use with caution!

This operation requires a [`Verified`](Sqlite.Auth.User#Verified) user. A user
can be verified by validating their password 
([`Sqlite.Auth.Password.validate`](Sqlite.Auth.Password#validate)) or their 
current session ([`Sqlite.Auth.Session.verify`](Sqlite.Auth.Session#verify)).

values.name: fromString
values.comment:
Turn a `String` into a raw [`Username`](#Username), ready to
[`normalize`](#normalize).

values.name: list
values.comment: Get all the usernames associated with a user.

values.name: migrationV1
values.comment:
Initial migration required for functions in this module to operate.

    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS usernames (
        username TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
        user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
        created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
        FOREIGN KEY (user_id)
            REFERENCES users(id)
            ON DELETE CASCADE
    );

`username` is, of course, the username of the user as a `String`. `user_id` 
references the user (in the [Sqlite.Auth.User](Sqlite.Auth.User) module). Both 
`created_at` and `updated_at` are posix timestamp values. `updated_at` is
updated appropriately whenever a username is [changed](#change).

This schema allows each user to have many usernames. If that's not desirable
for your application, you can add an additional migration to add a unique index.

    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS usernames_user_id_unique
        ON usernames (user_id);

values.name: new
values.comment:
Add a username to the given [`User`](Sqlite.Auth.User#User), returning 
the user for further pipeline steps. The passed username must be normalized 
using the [`normalize`](#normalize) function.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Sqlite.Auth.Username.Username Sqlite.Auth.Username.Normalized -> Sqlite.Auth.User.User -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error Sqlite.Auth.User.User

values.name: normalize
values.comment:
Ensures the username has been trimmed, is not empty, and all characters
are lowercase. This function does not remove internal spaces.

values.name: toString
values.comment: Get the underlying username `String`.

values.name: user
values.comment:
Get the user who owns the given username. Returns `Nothing` if the given
username is not associated with any user.
values.type: Sqlite.Database -> Sqlite.Auth.Username.Username Sqlite.Auth.Username.Normalized -> Task.Task Sqlite.Error (Maybe.Maybe Sqlite.Auth.User.User)
